en.title: Kahoot: reviewing the advanced labs
en.excerpt: The same content, playable in class (with Kahoot) or alone in the platform (no account needed).

tasks.title: Task 1: Lesson — how to review
tasks.content:
Reviewing is not re-reading: it is answering without looking.

This room is built for that: ten questions, a timer, and an explanation after every answer — including the wrong ones. In class you can go through Kahoot: same duration, same set of questions, and students play on their phones. Without a Kahoot account, the room works as it is.

Remember: a mistake that gets explained is worth more than a correct answer with no reasoning behind it. That is why every wrong option is commented.

questions.question: What is the best way to memorise a security concept?
questions.hint: What counts is recall, not reading.
questions.explanation: Explaining forces you to rebuild the logic, and therefore to spot the holes. That is why the rooms on this platform explain every mistake: spaced repetition does the rest.

questions.question: What is a classroom quiz useful for, beyond grading?
questions.hint: A quiz is a discussion tool.
questions.explanation: The value of a quiz is not the mark: it is the moment everyone discovers their blind spot, and the class talks it through. That is exactly what the platform does: the explanation is systematic.

tasks.title: Task 3: Mission — the proof of review
tasks.content:
The review left a trace on the dojo machine: /srv/briefs/07-revision.txt.

Mission. Open the document and pick out the value it states.

questions.question: Pick out the value from the review document.
questions.explanation: Same mechanics as everywhere else: a proof read inside the machine, compared by the server running as root.

tasks.title: Task 4: End-of-room exam
tasks.content: The ten quiz questions, timed. 60% is enough to pass.

questions.question: What is a threat model?
questions.explanation: The threat model is the foundation of any security work: you start from what you protect and what the adversary can do, then derive the mechanisms. Without it, you protect at random.

questions.question: What is a long but predictable password worth?
questions.hint: The number of combinations to try.
questions.explanation: Strength is measured in attempts. A long password multiplies the combinations to try: “chat1234” (8 characters) falls in a few hours on a single machine, while “Correct-Horse-Battery-9” (24) takes years.

questions.question: A SQL injection is…
questions.explanation: Injection comes from the missing separation: user data is concatenated into the query. It then becomes SQL code — and can read, write or delete.

questions.question: What is a firewall for?
questions.hint: A policy on what may pass.
questions.explanation: A firewall is a filtering rule set. It encrypts nothing and cleans nothing: it applies a traffic policy. A badly written rule lets through exactly what it was meant to block.

questions.question: “Least privilege” means…
questions.explanation: A service running with too many rights turns a bug into a disaster. Least privilege costs little to set up and limits the impact of a compromise.

questions.question: XSS is…
questions.hint: The script travels with the data.
questions.explanation: XSS stands for Cross-Site Scripting: the application reflects data back into its page without escaping it, and the browser runs the code. The consequence: a stolen session, or actions taken in the victim's name.

questions.question: What does the TLS certificate prove?
questions.explanation: Encryption protects against eavesdropping; the certificate protects against impersonation. Both are needed: HTTPS with no verified certificate only protects you from the network, not from a man in the middle.

questions.question: Hashing a password is…
questions.hint: You never read a hash back.
questions.explanation: A hash function is one-way. You check a password by recomputing its hash and comparing — hence the salt, so that two accounts with the same password do not share the same hash.

questions.question: How do you protect yourself from phishing?
questions.hint: Do not go through the link.
questions.explanation: Manual verification fails: a well-written message fools anyone. The most effective defence is mechanical: type the address yourself, or call the service on a number you already know.

questions.question: An exploited buffer overflow is…
questions.hint: What comes right after the buffer in memory.
questions.explanation: This is lesson 3 of course 6.858: the program does not check the size of the input. By overwriting the return address, the attacker chooses where the program continues. Hence the defences: canary, NX, ASLR.
